title: A Palace of Centuries
tagline: A schoolmaster in 1730 invented words made of dates. You will build a house with one room for every century and fill it with events.
card: A timeline palace: one room per century, the last two digits of each year as a picture, and the event as the scene.
goal: you will build a timeline palace with a room for each century, turn the last two digits of a year into a picture, and join it to the event.

left_off.q: What are the four small steps of memorising one item at speed?

left_off.a: The slowest step, which you should fix first.

left_off.q: When should you start timing yourself?
left_off.a: When you can do the task correctly at a slow pace.

text: England in the 1720s. A clergyman and schoolmaster, Richard Grey, has a problem every history teacher knows. His pupils can recite the story of the Norman Conquest, but they cannot tell you the year. They can name the kings, but not the order. Dates, he finds, are the first thing to fall out of a pupil's head.
A date is a number, and we saw in the second wing what the mind does with numbers: it lets go. Grey decided to do something about it.

check.q: What problem did Richard Grey notice among his pupils?
check.a: They could not hold on to dates. Numbers are the first thing to fall out of memory.

parts.talk: Which historical dates can you remember? How did you learn them?

text: In 1730 he published a small book called Memoria Technica, 'the technical memory'. In it he gave a code in which letters stood for digits, so that a date became a word, or a made-up word, which a pupil could learn like any other. The date of an event was hidden in a nonsense word that sounded a little like its name.

The strange words were never popular. They were clever but hard to learn: the code itself had to be memorised, and the words were dull. But the idea was sound, and it was the same as ours: turn a number into something you can say and see.

check.a: A 1730 book that used a code of letters for digits to turn dates into words, so pupils could learn them like words.

parts.talk: Why do you think the nonsense words were not popular?

text: We can do better with what we have. A date has two halves. The first two digits name the century; the last two name the year. There are only a few centuries that matter, and they can be rooms. There are a hundred possible year-endings, and they are the hundred pictures you already have from the number wing.

So a date becomes a place and a picture. The place is the century's room. The picture is the year-ending, joined to the event itself. For 1066: the room of the eleventh century, a judge (66), and a battlefield. You will see it, and you will not need to learn a nonsense word.

check.q: How does the timeline palace store a date?
check.a: The century is a room, the last two digits are a picture, and the event is the scene they act in.

parts.talk: How many centuries would you need rooms for, to cover the dates you care about most?

words.m: a period of a hundred years. The eleventh century is the 1000s.
in the order that things happened. A chronological list.
a line or list showing events in order of time.
something that happens, especially something important.
to take a country or place by force.
a length of time. A historical period.

source: Richard Grey's Memoria Technica was published in 1730. The details of his code are not needed here.
method_heading: Rooms for centuries, pictures for years

method.x: A year has two parts: the century (which room) and the last two digits (which picture).

items.x: A building with a room for each century you need, in time order from the front door. A twelve-room house covers the eleventh to the twentieth centuries and a bit more.
Use your Major System words (room 7): 66 = judge, 15 = doll, 92 = bone, 89 = fib, 69 = ship.
A few strong facts: who, where, what.

items.h: Join the year picture to the event.
items.x: In the century's room, the year picture acts in the scene.
From the oldest room to the newest. The order of events is the order of rooms.

method.title: 1066 in the eleventh-century room
lines: The eleventh century (the 1000s): the first room.
Norman soldiers and Saxon archers at Hastings.
A judge in a wig stands in the middle of the battle, banging a gavel, as an arrow hits his hat. 'Order!' he shouts at the Normans.
method.pic: A judge in a wig calling 'order!' in the middle of the battle of Hastings, with an arrow through his hat.

head: Year
Room
Year picture
Event scene
rows: A judge bangs a gavel at Hastings.
Barons force King John to sign a scroll with a giant doll's hand.
Columbus's ship has a giant bone for a mast.
A revolutionary tells a huge fib at the gates of the Bastille.
Napoleon trips over a lion's tail at Waterloo.
A silver ship lands on the moon with a flag.

items: Only the last two digits need a picture. The room carries the century.
Keep the event simple. One strong image of what happened.
Learn the sequence as a story as you walk from room to room: each event leads to the next.
Check by number sense. If it is the 1900s, you know the first two digits already.

method.x:
century = room.
last two digits = picture.
event = the scene.
Tell the scene for 1066 and one other date aloud, and name the room it lives in.

try.title: Year endings
try.prompt: Use the Major System. Match each year ending to a word.
Columbus sails across the Atlantic in 1492. The ending is 92 (bone or pen). Make a scene in the fifteenth-century room.
try.model: A tiny wooden ship, with a giant bone for a mast, sails into the room, and a flock of seagulls tries to eat the mast.
checks: The ending is a picture with the right sounds.
The event is in the scene.

try.title: 1789 and 1989
try.prompt: 1789: the French Revolution begins. 1989: the Berlin Wall falls. Both end in 89 (fib). Make two scenes that are very different from each other.
try.model: 1789 (18th-century room): a man in a powdered wig tells a huge fib at the Bastille, and his nose grows until it knocks over the gate. 1989 (20th-century room): people pull down a wall of cardboard bricks, laughing, while each brick says 'FIB' on one side.
checks: Each is in a different room.

try.title: 1969 and 1815
try.prompt: 1969: the Moon landing (69 = ship). 1815: Waterloo (15 = tail). Make a scene for each in its own century's room.
try.model: 1969: a silver ship lands in the moon-dust, with an enormous flag. 1815: Napoleon steps on a lion's tail on the battlefield, and the lion roars.
checks: Each is in the right room.
Each has the event and the ending picture.

items.s: The year 1066 belongs to the ___ century.
The year 1969 belongs to the ___ century.
The year 1492 belongs to the ___ century.

try.q: Why use a room per century?
opts: The order of events is built in, and the century is carried by the place
try.why: The place gives the century, and the walk gives the order.

try.title: A tour of the timeline
try.prompt: Tell the story of the six dates from the table, walking through the rooms in order.

cards: Battle of Hastings: the Normans conquer England.
Magna Carta is sealed by King John.
Humans first walk on the Moon.

quiz.q: In which century did the Berlin Wall fall?
What does the century's room tell you?
Which year is the French Revolution?
What gives you the order of the events?
quiz.why: The timeline walks from oldest to newest.

challenge.title: Memory challenge: seven years
challenge.intro: Learn these seven years in order: 1066, 1215, 1492, 1789, 1815, 1969, 1989. Walk through seven rooms. Type the years back, one per line.
challenge.study: Judge, doll, bone, fib, tail, ship, fib again: which room is each in?

look_back.q: How do you get faster at memorising?
look_back.a: Find the slowest step and make it automatic.

look_back.q: Name the five steps of the study cycle.
look_back.a: Understand, picture, place, test yourself, come back.

look_back.q: What is 66 in the Major System?
Why must a palace route be fixed?
look_back.a: The order of the places gives the order of the list.
